collections.label: 9.1 Energy
collections.learningIntention: Students will understand that energy vocabulary helps explain energy transfers, transformations, circuits, efficiency and future energy systems.
collections.successCriteria: Students can identify 9.1 Energy vocabulary from letter patterns, clues and definitions, then explain each term in a scientific context.

items.clue: The ability to do work or cause change.
items.definition: Energy is the ability to do work or cause change, such as movement, heating, light or sound.

items.clue: The idea that something remains constant overall.
items.definition: Conservation means that a quantity remains constant, even if it changes form or location.

items.clue: Energy cannot be created or destroyed.
items.definition: The Law of Conservation of Energy states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or transformed.

items.clue: A system where no energy enters or leaves.
items.definition: A closed system is a defined system where no energy is added or removed from outside.

items.clue: Energy moving from one object or place to another.
items.definition: Transfer is the movement of energy between objects, places or systems.

items.clue: Energy changing from one form into another.
items.definition: Transformation occurs when energy changes from one form into another, such as electrical energy becoming light.

items.clue: The energy of movement.
items.definition: Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.

items.clue: Stored energy due to position or condition.
items.definition: Potential energy is stored energy, often due to height, position, shape or chemical structure.

items.clue: Stored energy due to height in a gravitational field.
items.definition: Gravitational potential energy is energy stored because an object has been lifted above a lower position.

items.clue: Microscopic energy within particles.
items.definition: Internal energy is the total microscopic energy of particles in a substance, often linked to heating.

items.clue: Energy transferred because of temperature difference.
items.definition: Heat energy is energy transferred from hotter objects to cooler objects because of a temperature difference.

items.clue: Energy carried by vibrations through a medium.
items.definition: Sound energy is energy carried by vibrating particles through solids, liquids or gases.

items.clue: Energy transferred when a force moves an object.
items.definition: Work is the transfer of energy when a force causes movement over a distance.

items.clue: The rate at which energy is transferred or transformed.
items.definition: Power is the rate at which energy is used, transferred or transformed.

items.clue: The standard unit of energy.
items.definition: The joule is the standard unit used to measure energy.

items.clue: The unit used to measure power.
items.definition: The watt is the unit of power, equal to one joule per second.

items.clue: A unit of energy commonly used on electricity bills.
items.definition: A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy often used to measure household electricity use.

items.clue: How much input energy becomes useful output energy.
items.definition: Efficiency is the proportion of input energy that is converted into useful output energy.

items.clue: Energy supplied to a system or device.
items.definition: Input energy is the energy put into a system, machine or appliance.

items.clue: The desired energy produced by a system.
items.definition: Useful output energy is the energy transformed into the form wanted for the task.

items.clue: Energy transformed into unwanted forms.
items.definition: Wasted energy is energy changed into less useful forms, such as unwanted heat or sound.

items.clue: A force that opposes motion.
items.definition: Friction is a force that opposes motion and often converts kinetic energy into heat.

items.clue: A substance used to reduce friction.
items.definition: A lubricant reduces friction between moving surfaces, improving efficiency.

items.clue: Material used to reduce heat transfer.
items.definition: Insulation slows heat transfer and helps reduce wasted energy.

items.clue: Design features that reduce air resistance.
items.definition: Aerodynamics is the study or design of objects to reduce air resistance.

items.clue: A braking system that recovers some kinetic energy.
items.definition: Regenerative braking converts some kinetic energy into electrical energy during braking.

items.clue: Devices designed to minimise wasted energy.
items.definition: Energy-efficient technology provides the same useful output while using less input energy.

items.clue: How quickly a device uses or produces energy.
items.definition: Power rating shows the rate at which a device uses or produces energy.

items.clue: Using temperature change to estimate thermal energy.
items.definition: Calorimetry is a method used to estimate thermal energy by measuring temperature change.

items.clue: A factor kept the same in a fair test.
items.definition: A control variable is kept constant so an investigation tests the intended relationship.

items.clue: Energy used while an appliance is idle.
items.definition: Standby power is energy used when an appliance is plugged in but not actively being used.

items.clue: Technology that adjusts power use to improve efficiency.
items.definition: Inverter technology adjusts power output to improve energy efficiency.

items.clue: The total cost of owning and running something over time.
items.definition: Life-cycle cost includes purchase, operation, maintenance and energy costs across a product's life.

items.clue: A review of where and how energy is used.
items.definition: An energy audit examines energy use to identify waste and possible improvements.

items.clue: Controlling when and how energy is used.
items.definition: Demand management reduces pressure on energy systems by shifting or reducing energy use.

items.clue: To make the best or most efficient use of something.
items.definition: To optimise energy use means to make energy use more efficient, effective or sustainable.

items.clue: The origin from which usable energy is obtained.
items.definition: An energy source is the origin of energy used to perform work or generate electricity.

items.clue: Can be naturally replaced within a short time.
items.definition: Renewable resources can be naturally replenished on a useful human timescale.

items.clue: Cannot be replaced quickly once used.
items.definition: Non-renewable resources take a very long time to form and cannot be replaced quickly.

items.clue: Energy from sources that naturally replenish.
items.definition: Renewable energy comes from sources such as sunlight, wind, moving water and geothermal heat.

items.clue: Energy from finite resources.
items.definition: Non-renewable energy comes from resources such as coal, oil and natural gas.

items.clue: Energy sources used as alternatives to fossil fuels.
items.definition: Alternative energy refers to non-fossil or lower-emission sources such as solar, wind and hydro.

items.clue: Fuels formed from ancient living matter.
items.definition: Fossil fuels are coal, oil and gas formed from ancient organic matter over millions of years.

items.clue: Energy from the Sun.
items.definition: Solar energy is energy from sunlight that can be converted into heat or electricity.

items.clue: Energy from moving air.
items.definition: Wind energy is energy from moving air, often used to spin turbines.

items.clue: Energy from moving water.
items.definition: Hydroelectric energy uses moving or falling water to generate electricity.

items.clue: Energy from heat inside Earth.
items.definition: Geothermal energy comes from thermal energy stored beneath Earth's surface.

items.clue: Energy from organic materials.
items.definition: Biomass is organic material that can be used as a fuel or energy source.

items.clue: Splitting atoms to release energy.
items.definition: Nuclear fission releases energy by splitting large atomic nuclei.

items.clue: A gas released when many fuels are burned.
items.definition: Carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas released by burning carbon-containing fuels.

items.clue: A gas that traps heat in the atmosphere.
items.definition: Greenhouse gases trap heat in Earth's atmosphere and contribute to climate change.

items.clue: Total greenhouse gases linked to an activity.
items.definition: A carbon footprint is the total amount of greenhouse gas emissions caused directly or indirectly.

items.clue: Using resources responsibly for the future.
items.definition: Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations.

items.clue: Reliable and affordable access to energy.
items.definition: Energy security means having reliable, affordable and safe access to energy supplies.

items.clue: A policy or reward that encourages action.
items.definition: An incentive encourages certain actions, such as investing in renewable energy.

items.clue: Developing new ideas or technologies.
items.definition: Innovation is the development of new ideas, methods or technologies.

items.clue: A form of energy linked to electric charges.
items.definition: Electricity involves electric charges and can transfer energy through circuits.

items.clue: Energy carried by moving electric charges.
items.definition: Electrical energy is energy associated with moving electric charges.

items.clue: A property carried by electrons and protons.
items.definition: Charge is a property of matter carried by particles such as electrons and protons.

items.clue: The flow of electric charge.
items.definition: Current is the flow of electric charge through a conductor.

items.clue: The push that drives charges around a circuit.
items.definition: Voltage is the potential difference that pushes electric charges through a circuit.

items.clue: Another term for voltage.
items.definition: Potential difference is the energy difference per unit charge between two points.

items.clue: Opposition to the flow of current.
items.definition: Resistance is how strongly a component or material opposes current flow.

items.clue: A law linking voltage, current and resistance.
items.definition: Ohm's Law describes the relationship between voltage, current and resistance in a circuit.

items.clue: An instrument used to measure current.
items.definition: An ammeter measures electric current and is connected in series.

items.clue: An instrument used to measure voltage.
items.definition: A voltmeter measures voltage and is connected in parallel across a component.

items.clue: The unit used to measure current.
items.definition: Amperes are the units used to measure electric current.

items.clue: A device that converts chemical energy into electrical energy.
items.definition: A battery stores chemical energy and converts it into electrical energy.

items.clue: A machine that converts kinetic energy into electrical energy.
items.definition: A generator converts motion into electrical energy.

items.clue: A wheel with blades spun by wind, water or steam.
items.definition: A turbine spins when moved by wind, water or steam and can drive a generator.

items.clue: A device that converts light into electricity.
items.definition: A photovoltaic cell converts sunlight directly into electrical energy.

items.clue: A path through which electric current can flow.
items.definition: A circuit is a pathway that allows electric current to flow.

items.clue: A closed loop that allows current to flow.
items.definition: A complete circuit is an unbroken path that allows current to flow.

items.clue: A broken path that stops current.
items.definition: An open circuit has a break, so current cannot flow.

items.clue: A complete loop that allows current.
items.definition: A closed circuit provides a complete pathway for current to flow.

items.clue: A circuit with one path for current.
items.definition: A series circuit has components connected in one continuous path.

items.clue: A circuit with multiple branches.
items.definition: A parallel circuit has components connected across separate branches.

items.clue: A drawing that uses symbols to represent a circuit.
items.definition: A circuit diagram is a schematic drawing of a circuit using standard electrical symbols.

items.clue: A material that allows electricity to pass easily.
items.definition: A conductor is a material that allows electric charge to move through it easily.

items.clue: A material that resists electric current.
items.definition: An insulator is a material that does not allow electric charge to move through it easily.

items.clue: A circuit component that uses electrical energy.
items.definition: A load is a component that transforms electrical energy into another useful form.

items.clue: A device that opens or closes a circuit.
items.definition: A switch controls current by opening or closing a circuit.

items.clue: A separate pathway in a parallel circuit.
items.definition: A branch is one pathway for current in a parallel circuit.

items.clue: A component that limits current flow.
items.definition: A resistor is a component that provides resistance in a circuit.

items.clue: A label system for comparing appliance efficiency.
items.definition: Energy Star ratings help consumers compare the energy efficiency of appliances.

items.clue: A household device that uses energy.
items.definition: An appliance is a device such as a fridge, heater or washing machine that uses energy.

items.clue: A visual label showing relative efficiency.
items.definition: A star rating shows how energy-efficient an appliance is compared with similar appliances.

items.clue: Scores used to compare performance.
items.definition: Ratings are values or labels used to compare features such as efficiency.

items.clue: Standards used to make a judgement.
items.definition: Criteria are standards used to evaluate or compare options.

items.clue: The total energy used by a device or system.
items.definition: Energy consumption is the amount of energy used, often measured in kilowatt-hours.

items.clue: A label that helps compare appliance energy use.
items.definition: An energy label shows information such as energy use and efficiency for an appliance.

items.clue: A visual way to display data.
items.definition: A graph displays data visually so patterns and trends can be identified.

items.clue: The way data is shown visually.
items.definition: Visualisation is the presentation of data in visual forms such as graphs or charts.

items.clue: Changing presentation to mislead.
items.definition: Distortion occurs when data or visuals are presented in a way that misleads.

items.clue: Information collected from observations or measurements.
items.definition: Data is information collected through observations, measurements or research.

items.clue: A collection of related data.
items.definition: A dataset is a collection of related data values used for analysis.

items.clue: Information used to support or challenge a claim.
items.definition: Evidence is data or observations used to support a scientific explanation or conclusion.

items.clue: A statement that can be tested or evaluated.
items.definition: A claim is a statement that can be supported or challenged using evidence.

items.clue: The explanation linking evidence to a conclusion.
items.definition: Reasoning explains how evidence supports a claim or conclusion.

items.clue: The final judgement drawn from evidence.
items.definition: A conclusion is an interpretation or judgement based on evidence and reasoning.

items.clue: A preference that can affect interpretation.
items.definition: Bias is a tendency to favour one view, result or explanation over others.

items.clue: How information or data is shown.
items.definition: Representation is the way data or ideas are displayed, such as in graphs or diagrams.

items.clue: The amount of money needed.
items.definition: Cost is an important factor when comparing energy sources and technologies.

items.clue: The financial side of decision-making.
items.definition: Economics considers costs, benefits and resource use in decisions.

items.clue: The total amount of energy required.
items.definition: Energy demand is the total amount of energy needed by people, industries or societies.

items.clue: The combination of energy sources used.
items.definition: An energy mix is the combination of different energy sources used in a region or country.

items.clue: A digital electricity network that manages power flow.
items.definition: A smart grid uses digital systems to monitor and manage electricity supply and demand.

items.clue: A balance between emissions produced and emissions removed.
items.definition: Net-zero means total greenhouse gas emissions are balanced by removals from the atmosphere.

items.clue: Fair access to energy resources.
items.definition: Equity in energy means fair and reliable access to energy for all people.

items.clue: Electricity demanded from the grid.
items.definition: Operational demand is electricity demand supplied by the grid, excluding some behind-the-meter generation.

items.clue: Generation or storage on the customer side.
items.definition: Behind-the-meter systems include rooftop solar and batteries located at homes or businesses.

items.clue: The percentage of electricity from renewable sources.
items.definition: Renewables share is the proportion of energy or electricity generated from renewable sources.

items.clue: Energy used per unit of economic output.
items.definition: Energy intensity compares energy use with economic output or activity.

items.clue: Economic output per unit of energy used.
items.definition: Energy productivity measures how much value is produced for each unit of energy used.

items.clue: A possible future based on assumptions.
items.definition: A scenario is a modelled pathway based on assumptions about policy, technology and behaviour.

items.clue: A whole-of-system electricity roadmap.
items.definition: The Integrated System Plan is a roadmap for planning future electricity infrastructure.

items.clue: The consistent level of electricity demand.
items.definition: Base-load demand is the minimum continuous electricity demand that must be supplied.

items.clue: How consistently an energy source or system can supply energy.
items.definition: Reliability describes how dependable an energy source or system is over time.

items.clue: Changing with the seasons.
items.definition: Seasonal variation is change linked to different seasons, such as solar output across the year.

items.clue: Patterns that show change over time.
items.definition: Trends are patterns in data that show how something changes over time.

items.clue: Differences or changes within data.
items.definition: Variation describes differences or changes in data values.

items.clue: A lack of complete confidence in data or predictions.
items.definition: Uncertainty describes limits in how confident we can be about a result or prediction.

items.clue: Keeping energy for later use.
items.definition: Storage systems hold energy so it can be used later, such as batteries or pumped hydro.

items.clue: Making variable renewables more dependable.
items.definition: Firming uses storage, gas or other resources to make variable renewable energy more reliable.

items.clue: Moving bulk electricity over long distances.
items.definition: Transmission is the high-voltage network that moves electricity from generators to regions of use.

items.clue: Shifting systems from fuels to electricity.
items.definition: Electrification means replacing direct fuel use with electricity, such as electric vehicles or heat pumps.

items.clue: Average lifetime cost of producing electricity.
items.definition: Levelised Cost of Energy is the average cost of generating electricity over a technology's lifetime.

items.clue: Installed ability compared with actual output.
items.definition: Capacity is the maximum possible output, while generation is the actual energy produced.

items.clue: Money spent moving toward cleaner energy systems.
items.definition: Energy transition investment is capital used for clean power, grids, storage and related technologies.

items.clue: An observable or measurable indication of disease.

items.definition: Spread in respiratory droplets over short distances.

items.definition: Spread in small particles that remain suspended in air.

items.clue: Disease transmitted through contaminated water.
items.definition: Disease transmitted through contaminated water.

items.clue: Disease transmitted through contaminated food or toxins.
items.definition: Disease transmitted through contaminated food or toxins.

items.clue: A contaminated object that transfers pathogens.
items.definition: A contaminated object that transfers pathogens.

items.clue: A habitat in which a pathogen normally persists.
items.definition: A habitat in which a pathogen normally persists.

items.clue: A disease transmitted from animals to humans.
items.definition: A disease transmitted from animals to humans.

items.clue: The time between infection and the onset of symptoms.
items.definition: The time between infection and the onset of symptoms.

items.clue: The time during which an infected host can transmit a disease.
items.definition: The time during which an infected host can transmit a disease.

items.clue: An infected individual who can transmit a pathogen, sometimes without symptoms.
items.definition: An infected individual who can transmit a pathogen, sometimes without symptoms.

items.clue: Able to spread readily from one host to another.
items.definition: Able to spread readily from one host to another.

items.clue: A local increase in disease cases above the expected level.
items.definition: A local increase in disease cases above the expected level.

items.clue: A substantial regional increase in disease occurrence.
items.definition: A substantial regional increase in disease occurrence.

items.clue: An epidemic spreading across many countries or continents.
items.definition: An epidemic spreading across many countries or continents.

items.clue: Consistently present at an expected level in a population or region.
items.definition: Consistently present at an expected level in a population or region.

items.clue: The body system that recognises and responds to pathogens and abnormal cells.
items.definition: The body system that recognises and responds to pathogens and abnormal cells.

items.definition: Rapid, non-specific defence present from birth.

items.clue: Specific defence that develops after exposure to an antigen.
